title-group.article-title: Plant Community Characteristics Associated with the Occurrence of the Endangered Epiphytic Orchid Dendrobium moniliforme on a Coastal Cliff in Korea

abstract.p: Cliff habitats support distinctive plant communities, yet the vegetation characteristics associated with the natural occurrence of Dendrobium moniliforme remain poorly understood. This study characterized plant communities associated with the occurrence of D. moniliforme on a coastal cliff of Seonyudo Island, Republic of Korea, using unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-based vegetation surveys. A total of 56 plots, comprising 13 occurrence and 43 absence plots, were surveyed, and plant diversity, taxonomic composition, and life-form composition were compared between the two groups. Species richness was significantly lower in occurrence plots, whereas Shannon diversity was significantly higher. Plant community composition differed significantly between occurrence and absence plots (PERMANOVA, R2 = 0.075, p = 0.0005), with several species contributing to the observed compositional differences. Life-form composition also differed significantly between the two groups (PERMANOVA, R2 = 0.045, p = 0.028), with occurrence plots tending to show greater relative cover of chamaephytes, hemicryptophytes, geophytes, and epiphytes. These findings suggest that, within the studied coastal cliff, the occurrence of D. moniliforme is associated with differences in surrounding vegetation composition rather than simply greater species richness, providing site-specific baseline information for habitat characterization and conservation.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Cliff habitats are characterized by steep slopes, shallow and discontinuous soils, and limited availability of water and nutrients, creating harsh conditions for plant establishment and growth [1,2]. At the same time, variation in rock crevices, ledges, substrate characteristics, and topographic exposure creates considerable environmental heterogeneity at fine spatial scales, allowing plant species with different ecological requirements to coexist within relatively small areas [1,3]. These characteristics can support distinctive plant assemblages, including rare, endemic, and threatened species that are adapted to specialized cliff environments [3,4,5,6]. In coastal cliffs, additional environmental constraints such as salt exposure, drought, and differences in soil depth may further influence vegetation distribution and community composition [7]. Consequently, cliff habitats represent ecologically distinctive systems in which fine-scale habitat heterogeneity can play an important role in structuring plant communities.

Among plants occupying such heterogeneous habitats, epiphytic orchids often show non-random distributions because their establishment and persistence are influenced by substrate characteristics and local microenvironmental conditions [8]. D. moniliforme is a perennial orchid with a broad native range extending from the Himalayas to temperate East Asia, including Korea, China, Japan, and Taiwan, and occurs primarily as an epiphyte, although it can also grow on rocky substrates [9,10]. In Korea, D. moniliforme was assessed as Vulnerable (VU) in the 2020 Korean National Red List and has been legally protected as Class II endangered wildlife since 2012 under the Wildlife Protection and Management Act, with its designation maintained in the 2017 and 2022 revisions [11]. Previous studies have provided important insights into its reproductive biology and early development, including phenological growth stages, reproductive compatibility, mycorrhizal associations, and seed germination [12,13,14,15]. In particular, experimental studies have demonstrated self-incompatibility in D. moniliforme [13] and differences in fungal associations during seed germination and early seedling development [14], highlighting the complexity of its reproductive and establishment processes. In addition, studies on in vitro propagation have developed techniques for seedling production and ex situ conservation [16,17], while genetic investigations have revealed differentiation and geographical structure among East Asian populations [10,18]. Restoration studies in Korea have further shown that growth and vegetative propagation vary among planting substrates and microsites [9]. Despite these advances, and continuing conservation concerns related to habitat loss and collection pressure [11], information on long-term population dynamics and the vegetation characteristics associated with the natural occurrence of D. moniliforme remains limited.

Previous studies of coastal vegetation have demonstrated that plant community composition and distribution vary according to habitat characteristics and environmental gradients. In Korea, investigations of sea cliffs and other coastal habitats have documented differences in floristic composition and vegetation structure across coastal environments [19,20,21]. In particular, vegetation surveys on the coastal cliffs and adjacent plateaus of the Janggi Peninsula demonstrated that plant community distribution was associated with topographic and environmental conditions, including salinity, drought, and soil depth [7]. Similar studies on rocky coasts in Japan have shown that specialized coastal plant communities, including those supporting threatened and endemic species, are associated with particular site conditions [22]. These findings suggest that coastal cliff vegetation is structured by spatially heterogeneous environmental conditions and that differences in plant community composition may provide useful information for characterizing habitats occupied by threatened plant species.

The importance of surrounding vegetation has also been recognized in studies of epiphytic orchids. Their distribution and abundance can vary with host characteristics, vegetation structure, and local topographic conditions [23,24]. For example, epiphytic orchid communities have been associated with differences in surrounding tree density and the topography of host-tree sites [23], while studies of threatened Phalaenopsis species have highlighted relationships among host preferences, habitat vegetation, and spatial distribution [25]. Although these studies were conducted primarily in forest ecosystems, they suggest that the occurrence of epiphytic orchids may be associated with broader habitat and vegetation characteristics rather than host substrates alone. However, relatively little is known about whether similar associations occur in the natural habitats of D. moniliforme, particularly on coastal cliffs where vegetation develops under heterogeneous and restrictive environmental conditions.

Understanding the vegetation characteristics associated with D. moniliforme occurrence requires information on the diversity, taxonomic composition, and life-form composition of surrounding plant communities. Direct vegetation surveys on steep cliffs, however, are often constrained by limited accessibility, safety concerns, and substantial time and labor requirements [26,27]. Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-based surveys have emerged as a useful approach for investigating vegetation in inaccessible cliff habitats, allowing plant species and community patterns to be assessed remotely using high-resolution imagery [26,27]. Recent studies in Korea have further demonstrated the applicability of this approach for examining floristic patterns, life-form variation, and species composition on inaccessible island cliffs [28,29]. Nevertheless, these studies have primarily characterized cliff vegetation patterns rather than explicitly comparing surrounding plant communities between locations with and without D. moniliforme. Accordingly, UAV imagery provides an opportunity to investigate the vegetation characteristics associated with its natural occurrence in otherwise difficult-to-access coastal cliff habitats.

Therefore, this study aimed to characterize the plant communities associated with the natural occurrence of D. moniliforme on a coastal cliff of Seonyudo Island, Republic of Korea, using UAV-based vegetation surveys. Based on previous studies indicating that epiphytic orchid occurrence is associated with local habitat conditions and surrounding vegetation structure, we expected that plant community composition and life-form composition would differ between D. moniliforme occurrence and absence plots. In particular, we anticipated differences in the relative representation of epiphytic and woody life forms, reflecting variation in vegetation structure. We compared plant diversity, taxonomic composition, and life-form composition between D. moniliforme occurrence and absence plots to evaluate these expectations and identify vegetation characteristics associated with its natural occurrence within the study site. Through this approach, we sought to provide site-specific baseline information for understanding the ecological characteristics of its natural habitat and supporting its conservation and habitat management.

sec.title: 2.1. Study Area and Vegetation Survey
sec.p: The study was conducted on the rocky cliffs of Mangjubong, Seonyudo Island, Gunsan, Republic of Korea, in September 2025 (Figure 1). Seonyudo Island is part of the Gogunsan Archipelago, which is located approximately 50 km southwest of Gunsan on the western coast of the Korean Peninsula. The archipelago consists of 63 islands characterized predominantly by hilly terrain below 200 m above sea level [30]. The study site at Mangjubong consists of steep, exposed coastal cliffs, with vegetation occurring discontinuously in patches on the rock surface. Because direct access to the cliff faces was difficult, vegetation surveys were conducted using an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV; DJI Mavic 3T, DJI, Shenzhen, China).

The UAV was manually operated along accessible sections of the cliff face, with an effort to maintain an approximately 5-m distance from the rock surface. During the survey, the UAV was flown in both downward and upward directions (Figure 2a). Wide-angle imagery was acquired at vegetation patches along the cliff rather than at fixed intervals. The wide-angle camera (1/2-inch CMOS sensor, 48 MP, 84° horizontal field of view, 24-mm equivalent focal length) was used to obtain the primary imagery for vegetation assessment. When individual plant species could not be reliably identified from the wide-angle imagery, additional close-up imagery was acquired using the telephoto camera (1/2-inch CMOS sensor, 12 MP, 15° field of view, 162-mm equivalent focal length) to facilitate species identification (Figure 2b). Plant species were identified based on morphological characteristics visible in the UAV imagery, with reference to standard Korean floras [31,32,33]. D. moniliforme was identified based on its characteristic stem and leaf morphology rather than floral features.

Based on the approximate camera-to-cliff distance of 5 m and the horizontal field of view of 84°, the nominal image width was calculated as approximately 9.0 m using 2d × tan(θ/2), where d is the camera-to-cliff distance and θ is the horizontal field of view. Applying the image aspect ratio of 16:9 yielded an estimated height of approximately 5.1 m, corresponding to a nominal sampling area of approximately 45 m2. However, variations in camera-to-cliff distance and viewing angle may have occurred due to the irregular cliff surface and manual UAV operation. Therefore, the estimated area was used as a nominal reference rather than an exact measurement of the surveyed cliff surface.

All sampling units in which D. moniliforme was detected during the UAV survey were included as occurrence units, whereas absence units were selected from vegetation patches without D. moniliforme encountered during vertical UAV surveys along the cliff face. A total of 56 sampling units were examined on Cliff A, comprising 13 occurrence and 43 absence units. Each of the 56 vegetation sampling units was assessed using a distinct UAV image, with one image corresponding to each sampling unit. Plant species composition and cover-abundance were assessed from the UAV imagery using the Braun–Blanquet cover-abundance scale (r, +, 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5) [34].

GPS coordinates extracted from the UAV image metadata were used to characterize the spatial distribution of the 56 sampling units (Figure 3). These coordinates represent UAV camera acquisition positions rather than the exact locations or boundaries of vegetation patches on the cliff surface.

sec.title: 2.2. Vegetation Data and Life Form Classification
sec.p: Braun–Blanquet cover-abundance classes were converted to numerical values using a midpoint-based transformation (r = 0.01, + = 0.5, 1 = 3, 2 = 15, 3 = 37.5, 4 = 62.5, and 5 = 87.5). These values represent class-based cover-abundance estimates rather than directly measured percentage cover. D. moniliforme was excluded from the community dataset because occurrence and absence groups were defined by its presence.

To characterize the ecological composition of the cliff vegetation, all recorded plant species were classified according to Raunkiaer’s life-form system [35,36]. Species were assigned to eight life-form categories: mega-mesophanerophytes (MMs), microphanerophytes (Ms), nanophanerophytes (Ns), chamaephytes (Chs), hemicryptophytes (Hs), geophytes (Gs), therophytes (Ths), and epiphytes (Es). Life-form composition was calculated for each sampling unit based on the summed cover-abundance scores of species belonging to each life-form category and expressed as relative cover.

sec.title: 2.3. Data Analysis
sec.p: Species richness, the Shannon diversity index, and the Gini–Simpson diversity index (1 − D) were calculated for each sampling unit to compare alpha diversity between D. moniliforme occurrence and absence plots. The Shannon diversity index was calculated using the natural logarithm (ln) and species-level relative cover derived from the midpoint-transformed Braun–Blanquet cover-abundance values. The Gini–Simpson diversity index was calculated as 1 − Σpi2, where pi represents the relative cover of species i, using the same transformed cover data. Normality was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test, and differences in species richness, Shannon diversity, and Gini–Simpson diversity between the two groups were evaluated using Welch’s t-test. For each comparison, 95% confidence intervals for mean differences were calculated using Welch’s method, and standardized effect sizes were expressed as Cohen’s d. Species richness was additionally analyzed using a generalized linear model (GLM) with a log link and a Poisson error distribution. Because the data exhibited underdispersion, a quasi-Poisson model was used to account for the observed dispersion in the inference.

Differences in plant community composition between occurrence and absence plots were evaluated using non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) based on Bray–Curtis dissimilarities calculated from transformed Braun–Blanquet cover values of 39 associated plant species across 56 plots. A two-dimensional NMDS solution was used for ordination and visualization. Differences in community composition between the two groups were tested using permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA). Homogeneity of multivariate dispersion was assessed using PERMDISP to determine whether differences detected by PERMANOVA could be attributed to differences in within-group dispersion.

To examine potential spatial dependence among vegetation sampling units, Mantel tests were conducted to assess the relationships between geographic distances and Bray–Curtis dissimilarities in plant community composition. The analyses were performed for all sampling units and separately for occurrence and absence units. Geographic distances were calculated using GPS coordinates recorded at UAV image acquisition positions. To evaluate the sensitivity of the PERMANOVA results to spatial clustering, additional PERMANOVA tests were conducted using spatially restricted permutations. Sampling units were grouped into spatial blocks based on their geographic proximity using k-means clustering of geographic coordinates, and permutations were restricted within blocks. Sensitivity analyses were performed using 3, 4, 5, 6, and 8 spatial blocks. All permutation-based tests used 9999 permutations.

Similarity percentage analysis (SIMPER) was used to identify the plant species contributing most strongly to the Bray–Curtis dissimilarity between occurrence and absence plots. The contribution of each species to the average between-group dissimilarity was calculated, and species were ranked according to their percentage contribution.

Differences in life-form composition between occurrence and absence plots were also evaluated using Bray–Curtis dissimilarities. Relative cover values of the eight life-form categories were used to construct the life-form composition matrix, and differences between the two groups were tested using PERMANOVA. Homogeneity of multivariate dispersion was additionally assessed using PERMDISP. All statistical analyses were performed in R version 4.6.1 [37] using the vegan package version 2.7-5 [38] with statistical significance set at p < 0.05. To account for multiple testing, p-values from five primary comparisons (species richness, Shannon diversity, Gini–Simpson diversity, taxonomic composition, and life-form composition) were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure.

sec.title: 3.1. Plant Diversity and Community Composition
sec.p: A total of 39 co-occurring plant species, excluding D. moniliforme, were recorded across the 56 sampling units. Shapiro–Wilk tests indicated no significant deviations from normality for species richness (occurrence: W = 0.9234, p = 0.2788; absence: W = 0.9692, p = 0.2976), Shannon diversity (occurrence: W = 0.9631, p = 0.8013; absence: W = 0.9767, p = 0.5215), or Gini–Simpson diversity (occurrence: W = 0.9238, p = 0.2817; absence: W = 0.9815, p = 0.7079). Mean species richness was significantly lower in D. moniliforme occurrence plots (8.15 ± 1.91) than in absence plots (10.05 ± 2.25; Welch’s t = −3.002, df = 23.01, p = 0.0064; mean difference = −1.893, 95% CI = −3.197 to −0.589; Cohen’s d = −0.870). The quasi-Poisson GLM also indicated lower species richness in occurrence plots than in absence plots (dispersion parameter = 0.490; occurrence-to-absence richness ratio = 0.812, 95% CI = 0.699–0.942; p = 0.0059, FDR-adjusted p = 0.0079). In contrast, the Shannon diversity index calculated from midpoint-transformed cover-abundance values was significantly higher in occurrence plots (1.51 ± 0.31) than in absence plots (1.21 ± 0.31; Welch’s t = 3.053, p = 0.0063, FDR-adjusted p = 0.0079; mean difference = 0.297, 95% CI = 0.094–0.501; Cohen’s d = 0.970). Similarly, the Gini–Simpson diversity index (1 − D) was significantly higher in occurrence plots (0.686 ± 0.133) than in absence plots (0.536 ± 0.136; Welch’s t = 3.545, p = 0.0025, FDR-adjusted p = 0.0050; mean difference = 0.150, 95% CI = 0.062–0.238; Cohen’s d = 1.108) (Figure 4).

The two-dimensional NMDS solution based on Bray–Curtis dissimilarities had a stress value of 0.216 (Figure 5). D. moniliforme occurrence and absence plots showed substantial overlap in ordination space. Nevertheless, PERMANOVA revealed a significant difference in plant community composition between the two groups (F(1,54) = 4.3767, R2 = 0.07497, p = 0.0005, FDR-adjusted p = 0.0025). The occurrence–absence grouping accounted for approximately 7.5% of the variation in community composition, indicating a weak but statistically detectable difference between the groups. PERMDISP showed no significant difference in multivariate dispersion between the two groups (F(1,54) = 0.765, p = 0.3925).

Mantel tests revealed no significant relationships between geographic distance and plant community dissimilarity across all sampling units (r = 0.078, p = 0.081), occurrence units (r = −0.012, p = 0.506), or non-occurrence units (r = 0.011, p = 0.421). Spatially restricted PERMANOVA sensitivity analyses showed that differences in plant community composition between occurrence and non-occurrence units remained statistically significant across the examined spatial block configurations (3, 4, 5, 6, and 8 blocks; p = 0.0013–0.0271; Figure 6).

sec.title: 3.2. Species Associated with Community Differences
sec.p: SIMPER analysis identified the species contributing most strongly to Bray–Curtis dissimilarity between Dendrobium moniliforme occurrence and absence plots. Trachelospermum asiaticum (32.78%) contributed most, followed by Festuca ovina (16.69%), Davallia mariesii (11.61%), and Arundinella hirta (9.05%). Rhododendron mucronulatum (4.72%), Commelina communis (4.11%), and Lespedeza maximowiczii (2.85%) also contributed to the observed dissimilarity. The ten highest-contributing species collectively accounted for 88.53% of the average Bray–Curtis dissimilarity (Table 1).

sec.title: 3.3. Life-Form Composition
sec.p: Life-form composition differed significantly between D. moniliforme occurrence and absence plots (PERMANOVA: F1,54 = 2.530, R2 = 0.045, p = 0.028, FDR-adjusted p = 0.028). The occurrence–absence grouping accounted for approximately 4.5% of the variation in life-form composition. Occurrence plots tended to have higher relative cover of chamaephytes (Chs), hemicryptophytes (Hs), geophytes (Gs), and epiphytes (Es), whereas mega-mesophanerophytes (MMs), microphanerophytes (Ms), and nanophanerophytes (Ns) showed higher relative cover in absence plots (Figure 7). Therophytes (Ths) showed similar relative cover between the two groups. PERMDISP showed no significant difference in multivariate dispersion between occurrence and absence plots (F1,54 = 0.068, p = 0.793).

sec.title: 4.1. Plant Diversity and Community Composition Associated with D. moniliforme
sec.p: The occurrence of D. moniliforme was associated with distinct patterns of plant diversity and community composition on the surveyed coastal cliff. Species richness was significantly lower in occurrence plots (8.15 ± 1.91) than in absence plots (10.05 ± 2.25), whereas Shannon diversity (1.51 vs. 1.21) and Gini–Simpson diversity (0.686 vs. 0.536) were significantly higher in occurrence plots. This contrasting pattern suggests that plots supporting D. moniliforme contained fewer associated species but exhibited a more even distribution of relative cover among those species. Thus, lower species richness did not necessarily correspond to lower diversity when relative species abundance was considered.

The lower species richness in occurrence plots may partly reflect differences in vegetation structure and the representation of woody species. Several woody species were more prevalent in absence plots, whereas occurrence plots showed lower woody representation and relatively greater contributions from other life-form groups. These differences may be associated with variation in local habitat conditions, as substrate characteristics and topographic heterogeneity can influence vegetation composition within rocky habitats [3,24]. However, because these environmental factors were not directly measured, their contributions to the observed richness differences remain uncertain.

Plant community composition also differed significantly between occurrence and absence plots (PERMANOVA, R2 = 0.075), although occurrence status explained only a modest proportion of the total variation. Previous studies have reported associations between epiphytic orchid communities and surrounding vegetation or topographic conditions [25], while the growth and vegetative propagation of D. moniliforme have been shown to vary among restoration sites and substrates [9]. These findings provide ecological context for the observed community differences, but do not establish the environmental mechanisms responsible for them. Overall, our results suggest that D. moniliforme occurrence was associated with differences in surrounding species composition and relative cover rather than simply greater species richness.

sec.title: 4.2. Species Contributing to Community Differences
sec.p: SIMPER analysis identified several species that contributed to the compositional differences between D. moniliforme occurrence and absence plots. Trachelospermum asiaticum made the largest contribution (32.78%) and exhibited substantially higher mean numerical cover-abundance scores in absence plots than in occurrence plots (12.64 vs. 2.27). Other woody species, including Rhododendron mucronulatum, Lespedeza maximowiczii, Quercus variabilis, and Carpinus turczaninovii, also showed higher mean cover-abundance or constancy in absence plots. These findings indicate that differences in woody vegetation were an important component of the observed community dissimilarity.

In contrast, several herbaceous and fern species were common in both groups. Festuca ovina, Davallia mariesii, and Arundinella hirta contributed substantially to the SIMPER results, although their patterns of cover-abundance and constancy did not consistently favor occurrence plots. For example, Davallia mariesii showed slightly higher constancy in occurrence plots but higher mean cover-abundance in absence plots. These results suggest that community differences were not attributable to a simple replacement of woody species by herbaceous species or ferns, but instead reflected variation in the relative contributions of multiple taxa.

The relatively greater representation of several woody species in absence plots may also help explain the higher species richness observed in these plots. Previous studies have reported that vascular epiphyte composition can vary among microsites with different habitat conditions [24], while orchid communities may differ according to surrounding vegetation structure and tree species composition [39]. These findings provide ecological context for the observed differences in associated vegetation. Nevertheless, SIMPER contributions represent the contribution of each species to average community dissimilarity and do not establish that individual species directly promote or inhibit D. moniliforme occurrence. Therefore, the observed species associations should be interpreted as characteristics of the surrounding vegetation rather than evidence of causal interactions.

sec.title: 4.3. Life-Form Composition and Implications for D. moniliforme Habitat
sec.p: Life-form composition differed significantly between D. moniliforme occurrence and absence plots. Occurrence plots tended to have higher relative cover of chamaephytes, hemicryptophytes, geophytes, and epiphytes, whereas woody life forms (mega-mesophanerophytes, microphanerophytes, and nanophanerophytes) tended to have higher relative cover in absence plots. Rocky habitats contain heterogeneous microsites that differ in substrate availability and local environmental conditions, and such fine-scale heterogeneity can influence vegetation structure and the representation of different plant life forms or functional groups [40,41,42]. Therefore, the observed differences in life-form composition may reflect fine-scale variation in vegetation development and habitat structure within the cliff. This interpretation is also consistent with the SIMPER results, in which several woody species were more prevalent in absence plots.

The relatively greater representation of epiphytes in occurrence plots is particularly relevant because D. moniliforme is primarily an epiphytic orchid that can also grow on rocky substrates. The establishment and distribution of vascular epiphytes are influenced by water availability and can also be associated with variation in microclimate and substrate characteristics [43,44] and epiphytic orchid communities can also vary with surrounding vegetation structure and topographic conditions [25]. Thus, the differences in life-form composition observed in this study suggest that D. moniliforme occurrence may be associated with particular vegetation structures and microsite characteristics within the cliff, complementing the taxonomic differences observed between occurrence and absence plots.

sec.title: 4.4. Study Limitations and Future Directions
sec.p: Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings of this study. Vegetation sampling units were selected from patches encountered during UAV surveys rather than through systematic or randomized sampling. Accordingly, the observed vegetation patterns should be interpreted within the surveyed portions of the cliff.

GPS coordinates obtained from UAV imagery represented camera acquisition positions rather than exact vegetation patch locations. In addition, variations in camera-to-cliff distance, viewing angle, and cliff topography may have affected the actual sampling area. Consequently, the observed difference in species richness should be interpreted with caution because variation in actual sampling area could not be accounted for. Although Mantel tests detected no significant spatial relationships and spatially restricted PERMANOVA results remained significant, potential spatial dependence cannot be entirely excluded. The relatively small number of occurrence plots (n = 13) also warrants cautious interpretation of the observed differences.

The sampling scale was intended to characterize the surrounding vegetation rather than the immediate microhabitat of individual D. moniliforme plants, potentially obscuring fine-scale vegetation patterns. Small or obscured individuals may also have remained undetected in UAV imagery, resulting in possible false absences. Furthermore, because the survey was conducted only in September 2025, seasonal variation in species detectability and vegetation cover could not be assessed.

Despite these limitations, this study provides baseline information on plant communities associated with the natural occurrence of D. moniliforme in a coastal cliff habitat. Future studies incorporating repeated seasonal surveys, UAV-based three-dimensional reconstruction, improved imaging techniques, and smaller plant-centered quadrats paired with adjacent control plots could enable more detailed assessments of vegetation characteristics across spatial and temporal scales.

sec.title: 5. Conclusions
sec.p: This study demonstrated that the natural occurrence of D. moniliforme on a coastal cliff was associated with distinct characteristics of the surrounding vegetation. Species richness was lower in occurrence plots, whereas both Shannon and Gini–Simpson diversity indices were higher. Taxonomic and life-form composition also differed significantly between occurrence and absence plots, although occurrence–absence grouping explained relatively small proportions of the total variation. These findings suggest that D. moniliforme occurrence is associated with differences in surrounding vegetation composition and structure rather than simply greater species richness. The UAV-based approach also enabled vegetation characteristics to be assessed in an otherwise difficult-to-access cliff habitat.

From a conservation perspective, these results highlight the importance of considering not only D. moniliforme individuals but also the surrounding vegetation and habitat structure when characterizing and managing its natural habitat. Although this study focused on a single natural population, the vegetation patterns identified here provide baseline information for understanding the ecological context of D. moniliforme occurrence. Future studies across additional populations, combined with direct measurements of environmental variables such as light, moisture, and substrate characteristics, would help determine whether these vegetation patterns are consistently associated with D. moniliforme across its natural habitats.

caption.p: Location and overview of the study area on Seonyudo Island, Gunsan, Republic of Korea. (a) Geographic location of the study area on the Korean Peninsula; (b) satellite image showing the location of the study area on Seonyudo Island; (c) overview of Mangjubong Mountain with the rocky cliff area outlined by a red dashed line; (d) aerial view of Mangjubong Mountain showing the study area outlined in red; and (e) close-up UAV image of the coastal rocky cliff surveyed for D. moniliforme.

UAV-based vegetation survey on the coastal cliff. (a) Schematic illustration of the UAV survey approach along the cliff face. (b) UAV-acquired image used for vegetation assessment, with numbered areas (1–5) corresponding to enlarged images used for detailed species identification.
Spatial distribution of UAV image acquisition positions associated with D. moniliforme occurrence and absence sampling units on Cliff A, Seonyudo Island, Korea.

Comparison of alpha diversity in plant communities between D. moniliforme occurrence and absence plots. (a) Species richness, (b) Shannon diversity index (H′), and (c) Gini–Simpson diversity index (1 − D). Black dots represent individual sampling units (13 occurrence and 43 absence plots). p-values were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure.

Non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) ordination of plant communities in D. moniliforme occurrence and absence plots based on Bray–Curtis dissimilarities of transformed Braun–Blanquet cover values for 39 species across 56 plots (13 occurrence and 43 absence). Points represent individual plots, crosses (+) indicate group centroids, and shaded ellipses represent 95% confidence regions. NMDS stress = 0.216. PERMANOVA: F(1,54) = 4.3767, R2 = 0.07497, p = 0.0005; PERMDISP: F(1,54) = 0.765, p = 0.3925.

Spatial distribution of UAV-based vegetation sampling units under five spatial block configurations (3, 4, 5, 6, and 8 blocks). Colors indicate spatial blocks, while circles and triangles represent D. moniliforme occurrence and non-occurrence units, respectively.

Relative cover of plant life forms in D. moniliforme occurrence and absence plots. Bars represent mean relative cover (%), and error bars indicate standard errors (SEs). Mean relative cover was calculated from plot-level relative cover values across 56 vegetation plots (13 occurrence and 43 absence plots). MM, mega-mesophanerophytes; M, microphanerophytes; N, nanophanerophytes; Ch, chamaephytes; H, hemicryptophytes; G, geophytes; Th, therophytes; E, epiphytes.
Results of SIMPER analysis showing the major plant species contributing to the Bray–Curtis dissimilarity between D. moniliforme occurrence and absence plots.

fn.p: Note: Contribution represents each species’ percentage contribution to the average Bray–Curtis dissimilarity, and cumulative contribution represents the accumulated percentage contribution. Mean transformed cover value represents the average of cover values converted from Braun–Blanquet cover-abundance classes. Constancy represents the percentage of plots in which each species occurred. Δ Constancy was calculated as constancy in occurrence plots minus that in absence plots. Occ., occurrence plots; Abs., absence plots. Values are presented as mean ± SD. Numerical cover-abundance scores were derived from midpoint-transformed Braun–Blanquet classes and do not represent directly measured percentage cover.
